Title: The Heel Brake: A Certified Coach Swears By It, I Don't
Description: ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby teaches the heel brake as the first stop every inline skater should learn — every other method is harder to master. My own experience was rougher: it didn't always stop me in time, left my shin sore, and later got in the way of crossovers, so I take it off now. Two honest views, each attributed: teaching method from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby; personal account from me, Cass, a non-professional street skater. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Heel Brake: 3 Real Mistakes, Coached and Fixed
Description: A certified coach reviewed a real student's heel brake and found three fixable mistakes. Too-short scissor stance? Push the braking foot further forward. Slamming all your weight down? Keep 70% on your back leg, 30% on the brake, for a smooth slide. Straightening your back knee? Keep it bent, hips over your heel. (I'm not fully sold on this brake long-term — see my other post. Here's how to use it well meanwhile.) Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Heel Brake Fix Nobody Explains: Use Your Boot as a Lever
Description: The heel brake has an unfair reputation, usually from two fixable habits: not enough knee bend, and weight on the back of your foot instead of the front. The fix for both — push your shin into the boot cuff, using it as a lever, brake pad in front of your back skate's front wheel. Most who "hate" this brake never tried it. (I'm not fully sold on it forever — see my other post — but if you use it, this version works.) Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Spinning Out on a T-Stop Isn't a Strength Problem
Description: If your T-stop keeps turning into a spin instead of a slide, it's tempting to blame weak thighs. It's almost never that: too much weight on your sliding leg twists your hip, and your front skate pronates inward. Two drills fix both: the scissor glide, shifting 80% of your weight onto your back leg while lifting the front skate; and the toe roll, gliding on your front leg with trailing foot pointed back. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Build Your T-Stop With 2 Drills Before You Try the Real Thing
Description: The T-stop looks simple on an experienced skater, but it demands single-leg balance most beginners skip past. Most remove their heel brake and jump straight to a full T-stop — ending up with short, shaky slides. Build it in order instead: a static drill, 80% of your weight on your front leg, deep knee bend, back foot light enough to scrape; then a short rolling slide to build edge stability to a full stop. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Turning Stop Every Quad Skater Should Learn First
Description: The lunge stop is the prerequisite for two flashier moves — the powerstop and the lunge entry into a powerslide — reason enough to learn it well. Often confused with the easier parallel turn, a different technique. The goal: tighten your turn to roughly a one-metre diameter, which is what stops you. Quad skate technique from Asha Kirkby, a champion figure skater who represented Great Britain internationally and now teaches through Skatefresh. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Lunge Stop, Powerstop, or Powerslide: Which One Comes Next?
Description: Once your lunge stop is solid, two flashier stops open up from the same base: the powerstop, and the lunge entry into a powerslide. Both start from the same turning position — the lunge stop is the prerequisite for both, not a separate detour. Each has its own trade-offs in speed, control and space, worth knowing before you pick which to train next. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby, from her most-watched stopping tutorial.
